**HASH supports turning raw information into knowledge and process graphs, helping create graph-backed _world models_ that power process automation, optimization, decision making, and AI.** In essence, HASH is a self-building, open-source database which grows, structures and checks itself. Integrating data in (near-)realtime, it provides a powerful set of interfaces so that information can be understood and used in any context. Intelligent, autonomous agents can be deployed to grow, check, and maintain the database, collating and structuring information from the public internet — as well as your own connected private sources — in a standardized semantic form. Users, including those who are non-technical, are able to visually browse and manage both entities (data) and types (schemas). HASH acts as a source of truth for critical data, no matter its source, and provides a platform for high-trust, safety-assured decision-making. Read our blog post →

Many of HASH's features are unique to a platform of its kind, including its support for bitemporality, which provides first-order support for recording and querying both when something happened and, separately, when it became known. This capability is central to our support for better process modeling.
Instructions for using HASH can be found in the HASH Developer Docs.

The architecture guide walks through the full pipeline step by step.

**What it covers.** MCP tools (`mcp__*`, except mcp-recall's own) and the native Bash tool. Each output is routed to a handler built for its shape, so `git diff`, test runners, compilers and `grep` get summaries that put failures and errors first. The handler reference lists every handler and what it keeps. A result that carries an image, such as a browser screenshot, is delivered unchanged, since a text summary can't carry the picture. The built-in Read, Grep and Glob pass through unchanged; if large file reads are your biggest cost, the filesystem MCP server can be intercepted where Read can't.

- **Credentials are never stored.** Password-manager MCPs (1Password, Bitwarden, Vault and others) are blocked by name, credential-like tool names (`*secret*`, `*token*`, `*api_key*`, …) by pattern, and every output is scanned for secrets (PEM headers, GitHub PATs, AWS keys) before any write. A tool blocked by mistake goes in `denylist.allowlist`. Full lists: SECURITY.md.
- **Running alongside rtk:** its command-rewriting hook was measured with mcp-recall, and the install guide says what changes. Its PostToolUse pipeline is untested.

Without it, Claude Code puts an MCP result into the window whole when it is under 25,000 tokens (`MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`) and 50,000 characters. A larger result is saved to a file that Claude reads in chunks. Neither can be searched in a later session. mcp-recall swaps the result for a summary before it reaches the window and keeps the full output searchable. If Claude Code has already saved the result to a file, mcp-recall stores and summarizes the file's content instead of the notice.
|**① Tool definitions:** every connected MCP server loads its full schema up front, about 500 tokens per tool|Claude Code Tool Search (built in) · Switchboard|
|**② Multi-step workflows:** each intermediate result passes back through context|Code Mode · FastMCP 3.1|
|**③ Large MCP results:** in the window whole, or in a file read in chunks|**mcp-recall**|
|**④ Earlier sessions' output:** gone, or at best a model-written summary|**mcp-recall** keeps it verbatim and searchable (it is not a memory layer)|

In the API, context editing, compaction and the memory tool also reduce context, by dropping old content or summarizing it. None of them keeps the original output retrievable, and all of them work alongside mcp-recall.
